Markdown in AI workflows A single format carrying three of the six context types: Knowledge, Instructions, and Memory. A plain text file with nothing mechanical underneath. What matters is how and when it is consumed: as knowledge, as instructions, as memory — and whether the agent pays for it on every turn or only when it reaches for it. docs/handbook/onboarding.md Retrieved on demand Front matter header What is front matter? --- type: Handbook stale_after: 2026-07-01 owner: "@people-ops" --- Document body What is the body? # Employee onboarding Handbook for first-week setup. Dynamic context: the agent pays token costs only when a question reaches for it. 1. Collect laptop from IT on day one 2. Complete security training module 3. Meet your onboarding buddy Retrieved on demand. Stale pages answer just as fluently as fresh ones. Knowledge Retrieved on demand Pay only when fetched Show details onboarding.md · wiki · docs ↗ Instructions User or model invoked Progressive disclosure Show details commit · skills · commands ↗ Memory Always loaded Paid on every turn Show details AGENTS.md · CLAUDE.md ↗

Where the effort goes What a machine can check, what AI can help with, and what only a human can check. Three boundaries: what a machine automates, what AI accelerates, and what only a human can decide. machine deterministic cheap fast human non-deterministic time consuming trust AI non-deterministic AI judging token cost the AI region is my hypothesis — still unsettled

What the machine verifies Syntactic and structural checks that run deterministically in milliseconds without an LLM. Machine check Resolves cleanly ✓ Syntax: valid YAML frontmatter delimiter (---) & structure ✓ Resource: present and well-formed URI (https://intranet.example.com/people-ops/handbook#onboarding) ✓ Staleness: 2026-07-01T00:00:00Z parses with valid ISO timestamp Machine checking proves the file is mechanically sound. It cannot determine if the policy is still active.

What AI accelerates Cross-referencing prose against source handbooks to flag discrepancies for human review. Machine check ✓ Resolved cleanly AI recommendation ⚠ Discrepancy flagged (needs check) Observation Compared onboarding.md against linked People Ops handbook. Section 4 of the handbook updated equipment lead times from 5 working days to 7 working days. Proposal Recommend updating line 15 and notifying the hiring manager. The recommendation is rapid and insightful, but remains an unverified claim itself.

What remains human Is the policy still in force? Is the owner correct? Ground truth that no machine or model can know. Machine check ✓ Resolved cleanly AI recommendation ⚠ Discrepancy flagged Human judgment Open · Unresolved ? Does the buddy coffee on day one still match team practice? ? Does People Ops still close provisional accounts on Friday 5pm? ? Is the stated owner (@people-ops) still the accountable team? Ground truth that no machine or language model can know. You are the one accountable when it is wrong.

Google OKF Full OKF v0.2 frontmatter schema governing provenance, trust, and lifecycle. A standardized frontmatter schema to govern AI knowledge bases. Provenance, trust tiers, and lifecycle fields sit directly in markdown alongside the content. 1 --- 2 # --- Provenance (§5.1) --- 3 title: <Concept name> # REQUIRED — Human-readable concept title 4 version: 0.2.0 # SemVer concept version 5 description: <Summary> # Summary statement for agent indexing 6 tags: [onboarding, ops] # Categorical indexing keys 7 sources: # Optional — materials this concept derives from 8 - id: <citation-key> # Stable citation key for claim attribution 9 resource: <URI> # REQUIRED within entry — URI or path 10 # --- Trust (§5.2, §5.3) --- 11 generated: # Content production record 12 by: <Actor> # REQUIRED within generated — agent or human 13 at: <ISO 8601> # Timestamp of generation 14 verified: # Content verification event log 15 - by: <Actor> # REQUIRED — reviewer who sets trust tier 16 at: <ISO 8601> # Timestamp of verification 17 # --- Lifecycle (§5.4) --- 18 stale_after: <ISO 8601> # Temporal expiration date 19 owner: "@people-ops" # Accountable team or user 20 --- OKF Official Open Knowledge Format Specification (v0.2) Open specification by Google Cloud Platform for agent-maintained knowledge repositories. Markdown in AI workflows Three context types Markdown carries Knowledge, Instructions, and Memory with distinct lifecycle and retrieval costs. Consumption cost What matters is whether the agent pays context tokens on every turn or retrieves on demand.

Volume outruns review Decay and drift crossing On a single document, maintenance effort decays while drift climbs — that crossing is where the work moved. Compounding surface Across a corpus, the verification surface multiplies faster than the raw file count.

Where the effort goes Three boundaries Document verification is three distinct jobs: deterministic machine checks, AI acceleration, and human judgment. Division of labour Push mechanics to the machine and discovery to AI so humans only handle genuine judgment calls.

What the machine verifies Deterministic checks Syntax, schemas, dates, and URIs validate deterministically in milliseconds without an LLM. Mechanical ceiling A clean pass proves structural integrity, never that the underlying statement is true.

What AI accelerates Cross-referencing prose AI can follow references across files and flag contradictions for human review. Signals, not truth The AI recommendation is rapid and insightful, but remains an unverified claim itself.

What remains human Ground truth and policy Whether a policy is active or an owner is correct requires ground truth outside the repository. Accountability Tooling narrows the decision surface, but accountability stays with the human.

Google OKF Shared metadata standard OKF v0.2 standardizes frontmatter fields for AI knowledge bases. Governance fields Provenance, trust tiers, and lifecycle sit directly in markdown next to the content.

Steering the AI Raising the floor A document can declare how much of itself to believe; reliable signals warn when humans must step in. Stopping before judgment markdown-harness steers the machine layer and prepares signals without claiming human judgment.

Runs on a 100% deterministic core Three triggers, one core Pre-read agent hook, pre-commit gate, or manual check all execute the identical deterministic core. Deterministic evaluation Configuration and file inputs produce the exact same verdict every run.

Live demo Comparative evaluation Three agents receive the same stale document; only the hooked agents are prevented from hallucinating outdated facts. Live terminal run Talk switches to terminal here; the slide acts as the anchor framing the test.

Feature Roadmap Current release (v0.0.4) Shipped: frontmatter linting, staleness checks, and markdown-harness skill. Planned capabilities Future: drift detection and corpus validation; do not promise them as shipping today.

The verifying half is yours The work moved Writing docs is automated; verifying them is the real work, and it belongs to you. Summary thesis Machines verify structure, AI accelerates cross-references, and human judgment owns accountability.

Markdown in AI workflows 0:00 – 0:28 The agentic era not 2023 local files tools loops Before we start, I want to establish why markdown files matter so much in AI workflows. We're in the agentic era now — it isn't 2023 anymore. Agents aren't chatbots you copy-paste into. They read files on your machine, write files, call tools, search the web. Put those in a loop and they carry out real tasks, the way the new colleague you just onboarded would. 0:28 – 1:14 Three categories of markdown knowledge instructions memory silent failure And like that colleague, an agent needs the right information at the right time. That information lives in markdown — which is just a plain text file. Those files fall into three categories. Knowledge — what the agent looks up on demand, when the task calls for it. Instructions — skills: how to do a release, step by step, written once and called by name. And memory — not ChatGPT's memory, but a file the agent reads at the start of every single conversation. And if that file is stale, or wrong, the agent reads that wrong information every single time. Confidently, and silently — without you ever noticing. Bridge And that's one document.

Volume outruns review 0:00 – 0:39 Effort decay and drift decay curve effort drops drift climbs maintenance budget And that's one document. There's a reason knowledge management was always hard in enterprise — long before any of this. And it's this shape. One document, over time: the blue line is effort. There's a spike at the start, when someone writes it. At least, that's how it used to be — with AI, creating a document now costs almost nothing. After that, effort drops. Because nobody budgets for maintenance. It's never in the plan. And as effort drops, drift climbs. The document is still sitting there. It's just quietly stopped being true. 0:39 – 1:18 Corpus compounding accumulate steadily claims and references brake is gone Now scale that. Your documents don't arrive one at a time — they accumulate, steadily. And you're not just verifying each file. You're verifying every claim each file makes about the others. Every reference. That compounds. So here's what changed: writing was the brake. The human was the bottleneck — you could only produce documentation as fast as someone could write it, and that held the whole thing in check. That brake is gone. Bridge So the brake is gone. Which raises the obvious question: what does it actually take to check a document?

Where the effort goes 0:00 – 0:54 Three non-interchangeable tiers machine human AI deterministic to semantic It's not one job. It's three, and they're not interchangeable. On the left, the machine: deterministic — same input, same answer, every time. Binary: it passes or it fails. Cheap, and fast. This is the part you want doing as much as possible. On the right, the human: not deterministic, slow, expensive. This is where the semantic work happens — is this actually true, is it still useful. And it's still where almost all trust comes from. And in the middle, AI: it works in natural language, so it sits on the human side of that line — not deterministic. It costs tokens. What it can and can't be trusted with is genuinely unsettled. Bridge Left to right. Cheap and certain, to expensive and human. Let's take them in order.

What the machine verifies 0:00 – 0:43 What the machine verifies frontmatter metadata shape link checker ceiling Start with the low-hanging fruit. What can a machine check, every time, for free? Here's a markdown file — an onboarding process. At the top, the frontmatter: key-value pairs in YAML that carry metadata, mostly for the machine and the agent. Underneath, the body. A machine can check the shape of that metadata. Is the type declared. Is the date a real date. Is the link well-formed — and it can even follow it and see if it's still there. And that's the ceiling. It can tell you the field exists. It can't tell you whether what's written in it is true.

What AI accelerates 0:00 – 0:54 What AI accelerates contradictions cross-references tickets signals So what does AI add? It can follow that reference. Read the document on the other end. And notice that this one says five days and that one says seven. That's a contradiction it found on its own — and what it does with it matters more than finding it. It can flag that one section and raise a ticket, so a human resolves a single line instead of re-reading the document. Those are signals. Every signal narrows what a human actually has to look at. But can it make the call? It can produce one. It's like stopping someone in the street, handing them both documents, and asking which is right. You'll get an answer. If you own this process — would you trust that person?

What remains human 0:00 – 0:23 What remains human accountability ground truth always yours Which leaves this: is the coffee thing still how the team works? Is this person still the owner? No amount of tooling answers those. You have to know — and you're the one accountable when it's wrong. The machine narrows it. The AI narrows it further. What's left is the part that was always yours.

Google OKF 0:00 – 1:00 Google Open Knowledge Format OKF v0.2 shared vocabulary agent generated human verified lifecycle The machine finds structure. The AI adds a first layer of meaning, to help a human decide faster. And what's left was always yours. So let's go back to the machine half, and ask how we make it bigger. A machine works on structure. Which means it only works if we agree on a shared vocabulary. This is Google's Open Knowledge Format. It's open, and it's early — version 0.2, still moving. It names the fields, and says what each one means: type, title, description, sources, and the interesting ones: trust, and lifecycle. That a document was generated by an agent, and verified by a human. And stale_after — freshness. If we all agree to use the same vocabulary, the checker gets written once, and works everywhere. Bridge Which makes the machine's half a lot bigger than checking that a date is a date.

Steering the AI 0:00 – 0:53 Steering the AI markdown-harness raise floor steer arrow human boundary So the goal is to make the machine's half do more. And this is what I've been building over the past couple of weeks: markdown-harness. The idea is one sentence: a document can tell you how much of itself to believe. It's not about generating trust. Trust is semantic — a machine can never produce it. What it can do is raise the floor. Reliable signals that tell an agent or a human that something needs attention. You've seen these three circles before: deterministic, cheap, fast signals handed to the AI while it's working. The machine column reaching into the AI column. That's the arrow. And the human side is greyed out on purpose: this tool stops before it. That part was always yours.

Runs on a 100% deterministic core 0:00 – 0:45 One deterministic core three triggers runtime pre-read commit gate nightly schedule Three ways in. Three ways out. And the middle is the same every time. Whatever starts it, the core does one thing: read the configuration, run the logic. Same input, same answer. It's fully deterministic. The one I want to show you is the first: the agent goes to read a file — and before it does, it's told that file is stale. The other two, briefly: on commit, a check that the frontmatter meets the standard, passing or blocking. And on a schedule: a nightly run that regenerates what can be regenerated, and raises a ticket on what can't. Bridge Let me show you the first one.

Live demo 0:00 – 0:37 The check run live three terminals un-hooked pirate injection deny read Three panels: same question, same document. The only difference is what each one is allowed to know. Before the run: watch the un-hooked panel answering confidently from a document that went out of date. If it noticed the date, that detection was luck — dependent on the model. The injected panel: the pirate response proves the harness governed what the agent was allowed to know. The deny panel: read was refused explicitly. And deterministic detection was recorded in the log, independent of what any model chose to say.

The verifying half is yours 0:00 – 0:42 The verifying half is yours third time lit human region work moved always yours This is the third time you've seen this picture. First as what verification costs. Then as what the tool does — reaching into the middle, and stopping at the edge of the human. Same three circles. All that's changed is which one is dark. Machines check structure. AI accelerates drafting. And the work moved — to the part that was always yours. One thing I want to be straight about: the middle region is my hypothesis. How much an agent can be trusted with is not settled — an open problem. The tool's here if you want it. It's early. Thank you.
